newsitem.title: GERMANY: Analysts comments on future ECB credibility.
newsitem.headline: Analysts comments on future ECB credibility.

text.p: Here are comments from economists on the credibility of the future European central bank, following the release by the European Monetary Institute on Friday of details of its operational framework.

"There is reason to doubt that the future European central bank will be as successful as the Bundesbank in maintaining monetary stability and that emanates from the calls recently for a political counterweight to the central bank, and the calls for a weaker Euro to boost competitiveness.
It is very much a question of how the whole economic framework develops and whether the public shares the central bank's determination to keep inflation low.

The Bundesbank did not build its reputation on the fact that it had a Lombard rate or minimum reserves -- but on the fact that it was able to withstand political pressure for a looser monetary policy, which has come up in Germany many times.

On paper it all looks good (for the future European central bank) -- they are independent, they are only looking at price stability and the instruments that will be used are pretty similar to those which have been used by the Bundesbank .. But there could be a real difference between this technical framework and the practice.
The key question is -- will the ECB be able to fend off political pressure for lower interest rates?"
DARREN WILLIAMS, EUROPEAN ECONOMIST, UBS, LONDON
"Given that most of European central banks are set up similarly to the Bundesbank, it won't make any difference to the ECB from a credibility standpoint if its tools are similar to the Bundesbank.

I think the real question is the French suggestion for a kind of separate stability council on a political level, which is kind of a separate development. France really has made no secret that it wants this and I personally think this is going to be the key issue in this whole European debate in 1997, like the stability pact was last year.

The independence of the central bank will actually be helped by its decision to exclude an exchange rate target (as an option for monetary targeting) but this will not be enough. Until these things are clear, I think it will be 1999 or 2000 before we can make a real judgement on the credibility factor."
THOMAS MAYER, SENIOR ECONOMIST, GOLDMAN SACHS, FRANKFURT

"The main problem is going to be the level of political interference in monetary policy under monetary union. What the Bundesbank has done carefully over the years is deflect this tendency and this is what the ECB is up against if it wants to follow in the footsteps of the Bundesbank.

People often say of the Bundesbank that it 'forms' its council members, no matter what region they come from or interests they represent. The ECB will have to develop this kind of corporate identity too but whether it can do that is totally up in the air.
In Germany, a situation has developed that when it comes to monetary policy, politicans keep their hands off, but other countries have other habits and other ideas.
France and Germany have a completely different understanding of exchange rate policy, for example.

If this stability council (as suggested by the French) is set up specifically to act as a political counterweight to the European Central Bank, then of course the central bank could be restricted and would not be able to follow in the Bundesbank's footsteps -- but this is a question that has not yet been decided.
The preconditions are there for a stable Euro, but the question is are enough of the necessary conditions in place?
